(1)
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Governors Safer Communities Initiative brings
together governors who are committed to championing
whole-of-government strategies that build safer communities and prevent gun violence in their respective jurisdictions.1  Governors formed the Safer Communities Initiative to implement innovative cross-state approaches to
keeping their communities safe.
The Governors Safer Communities Initiative includes
California Governor Gavin Newsom, Colorado Governor
Jared Polis, Delaware Governor Matt Meyer, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, Maryland Governor Wes Moore, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, New York Governor Kathy
Hochul, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, Rhode Island Governor Daniel McKee, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, and Washington Governor Bob Ferguson.  Given
its priorities, the Initiative’s members have a significant
interest in the defense of common -sense measures that
regulate possession of certain dangerous weapons.  Al -
though the laws of amicus members’ jurisdictions differ
in substance, we are aligned in our firm conviction that
states retain broad authority under their police power to
enact measures like these —tailored to their own residents’ needs and consistent with our Nation’s historical
tradition. The officials who enact them, moreover, are
best positioned to judge what their communities need.
Amicus members’ jurisdictions have confronted,
firsthand, the human and operational consequences of
mass shootings committed with assault weapons—in New
York, at Buffalo; in Illinois, at Highland Park; in Colorado, at Colorado Springs; in California, at Monterey

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part. No

2

Park, and in other Initiative members’ jurisdictions that
have lived through similar tragedies.  As the chief executives responsible for their states’ emergency response,
public health, and victim-services systems, amicus members write to provide the Court with a firsthand account
of what these shootings have cost their communities, and
why the laws at issue reflect a considered, evidence-based
response to a real and recurring threat to public safety.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
For the governors of the Safer Communities Initiative, the question presented in this case is not an academic
one.  Amicus governors have had to decide, in the days
and weeks after an assault -weapon attack in their own
state, how to mobilize the human and financial capacity to
respond to a tragedy no community should have to endure.  Four such attacks are recounted below from  the
perspective of the chief executives responsible for the
safety of their communities.
Virtually all of amicus members’ jurisdictions have
experienced a mass shooting—in their houses of worship,
grocery stores, suburban malls, schools—bearing the burden of law-enforcement mobilization, emergency medical
care, victim compensation, and a disruption to community
life reaching well beyond the shooting scene itself.  These
costs are neither speculative nor short -lived.  State response to mass shootings alone runs into the hundreds of
millions of dollars nationwide; the broader cost of treating
firearm injuries reaches into the billions.  Both continue
long after the headlines fade.
The extraordinary human and financial toll is a direct
consequence of what assault weapons are built to do.
These are weapons explicitly designed for the battlefield,
adopted by the U.S. military in the 1960s and still in use
to this day.  These weapons are outfitted for our troops
with the features included in the Cook County Ordinance

3

and Connecticut Statute at additional expense, because of
the express tactical advantages that give them a capacity
for mass casualties far exceeding that of an ordinary firearm.  States and the federal government have regulated
these weapons for decades, frequently in direct response
to the kind of tragedy amicus governors describe below,
and the empirical record confirms that legislative judgment: jurisdictions that have enacted assault -weapons
safety measures experience fewer, and less lethal, mass
shootings than those that have not.
Taken together, amicus governors’ firsthand experience and the empirical record confirm that the Cook
County Ordinance at issue in this case and the Connecticut law at issue in the companion case reflect precisely the
kind of considered, evidence -based judgment that the
Constitution—from the founding to the modern era —
leaves to the states’ traditional police power.  The judgments below should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. Amicus Members Have Directly Confronted the
Human Costs and Operational Consequences of
Assault-Weapon Violence
A. Amicus member governors have personally
experienced the human toll of assault-weapon
violence in their own states
The overwhelming majority of Governors Safer Communities Initiative members’ jurisdictions have experienced a mass shooting—the victims were their own neighbors, coworkers, and classmates.  Governors were called
to answer these attacks with the emergency r esponders,
hospitals, and victim -services systems their states had
built.  The accounts that follow recount several such tragedies and the devastation they caused, from the perspective of the state’s chief executive charged with keeping its
residents safe.

4

1.  On May 14, 2022, an eighteen -year-old gunman
drove more than three hours from his home in Conklin,
New York, to a Tops Friendly Market on Jefferson Avenue in Buffalo, deliberately targeting a supermarket in
the city’s predominantly Black East Side neigh borhood.2
He was armed with an assault rifle that he had illegally
modified to accept a large-capacity magazine.3  In roughly
six minutes, he killed ten people—all of them Black—and
wounded three others.4
On the day of the attack, Governor Kathy Hochul, a
Buffalo native, told reporters, “This is my community. I
know this community well, I’ve walked these streets.” 5
She described a neighborhood’s “sense of security shattered” by a “military style execution,” targeting people
who simply wanted to buy groceries. 6  The next day, she
spoke of the “excruciatingly painful process” of identifying the victims and notifying their families 7 and ordered
flags lowered statewide, declaring that “[a]n attack on one

II. Assault Weapons Make Mass Shootings More Lethal,
and Safety Measures Regulating Them Work
A. Assault weapons are distinctively dangerous, and
safety laws regulating their use save lives
1. Assault weapons are firearms engineered with a
specific set of combat-functional features that, taken together, produce a “capability for lethality—more wounds,
more serious, in more victims —far beyond that of other
firearms in general, including other sem iautomatic
guns.”  Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 453 (4th Cir.
2024) (en banc), cert. denied sub nom. Snope v. Brown,
145 S. Ct. 1534 (2025) (quoting Kolbe v. Hogan, 849 F.3d
114, 125 (4th Cir. 2017) (en banc) , abrogated on other

597 U.S. 1 (2022)).  The AR-15 sold to civilians today is the
paradigmatic example.   That weapon was explicitly designed for the battlefield, with “combat -functional features” including a flash suppressor (to conceal the
shooter’s position), a pistol grip (to “enable fast reloading
and accuracy” during prolonged firing), and exceptional
firepower (to pierce helmets and body armor).  See Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 454–456.
The ability to accept a large -capacity magazine
(LCM) frequently plays an integral part in the assault
